newsitem.title: GERMANY: Czech gvmnt holds key to rate policy - cenbank head.
newsitem.headline: Czech gvmnt holds key to rate policy - cenbank head.

text.p: Czech central bank governor Josef Tosovsky on Monday said that government policies could become a linchpin for interest rate levels and that further steps would likely be a precondition to easier monetary policy.

At a time when one senior central bank official has said the crown should be trading near its dollar/mark basket parity and not its current +1.5-2.0 level, talk of central bank intervention, possibly including a rate cut, has resurfaced.

Asked whether and when the central bank might consider such a step, Tosovsky was studiously neutral, saying the central bank had several options and that much could depend on future government policies.

"For us it is important to keep overall aggregate demand under control. This will contribute to stabilisation and in the future to a reduction of imbalances in foreign trade," Tosovsky said, explaining this was a reason for recent restrictive policies.
"But without some other measures taken by other partners (the government) it would be difficult to abolish this policy," Tosovsky added.
The central bank last raised its discount rate by one full percentage point to 10.5 percent last summer.
The central bank was currently completing a reassessment of economic developments at a time when certain trends, including the rise in wages, were not sustainable, Tosovsky said.
Declining to be drawn out on possible specific action, he said one of the central bank's priorities was to achieve a "good policy mix", including government policies.
One particularly worrying trend was a 17.4 percent rise in nominal wages, which Tosovsky said "can't continue like that and must be put closer in line with production".
Although fast wage growth had been partly justified since the end of Communism, Tosovsky left no doubt that the current pace cannot be supported by the economy.
While a return to regulated wage increases would not be desirable, Tosovsky said that he could imagine more effective ways of guiding wage increases.

As no new mechanisms were put in place after wages were completely deregulated, Tosovsky questioned how effective and potentially dangerous the current system might be. "It is worthwhile thinking about these things," he said.
On the other hand Tosovsky said the central bank was still sticking by its eight percent inflation rate target for this year, even after the government last week announced several price deregulation.
Noting that inflation had come down as the central bank had been successful at controlling money supply growth, Tosovsky said he saw no reason to alter the inflation outlook.

"We won't change our plan, we are sticking by eight percent," Tosovsky said, even though he admitted that the headline inflation figure might rise after the price deregulation take effect during the course of the year.
On Friday Czech Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik revised upwards the government's 1997 inflation outlook to 9.5 percent after the ruling coalition parties moved to ease Communist-era price controls.
Average annual inflation was 8.8 percent last year and Tosovsky said the nation had recently enjoyed an easing in price growth.
Government coalition partners last week agreed to increase rent prices on state-controlled housing and to raise value added tax on gas and electricity to 22 percent from five percent from July 1.
